chunks: From him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Salih ibn al-Sindi, from Ja'far ibn Bashir, from al-Husayn ibn Abi al-'Ala', from Abu 'Amr al-Sarraj, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him).
Regarding the man in whom theft is found, he said: 'He is indebted if he does not bring witnesses to the one who sold it.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on stolen goods found in someone's possession if they claim to have bought them?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the presumption of liability (*gharam*) for a possessor of stolen goods, shifting the burden of proof to them to establish a valid purchase. In Shia jurisprudence, this highlights the principle that mere possession of an item suspected to be stolen does not automatically prove theft, but rather creates a financial debt to the original owner until the buyer proves their good faith acquisition through witnesses. This ruling protects the rights of the original owner while providing a mechanism for innocent purchasers to clear their liability.
